nodes.label: The BeOS Bible (Scot Hacker, Peachpit Press, 1999)
nodes.author: Scot Hacker
nodes.rationale: The source this whole document references by chapter.

nodes.label: The Giampaolo interview
nodes.rationale: The source for BFS's history, the three always-indexed attributes and People files.

nodes.label: Client/server architecture
nodes.rationale: BeOS split system functions into servers by category; the argument is economy, so clients do not spend cycles doing redundant work. Kosmos takes it further: in BeOS the servers shared a monolithic kernel with the drivers and the filesystem inside it, and in Kosmos they are processes with separate address spaces talking over kernel IPC.

nodes.label: Pervasive multithreading - pushing sand, not rocks
nodes.rationale: Nobody computes faster, but everything responds better because everything gets constant attention in small pieces. Creating a BeOS window spawned two threads. Kosmos keeps the property - a busy window does not freeze the others - and changes the mechanism to coroutines.

nodes.label: BFS: a filesystem shaped like a database
nodes.rationale: BeOS used an actual relational database as its filesystem through DR8 and pulled it: too complex to maintain, too costly in performance. At DR9 they rewrote it as a directory hierarchy with attributes and an indexed attribute pool, lost very little and gained a lot of speed. The most useful warning in the book.

nodes.label: The three always-indexed attributes
nodes.rationale: BFS indexed name, size and modification date on every file, always, which is why a query by name was a targeted index lookup rather than a walk. Decision: those three are always indexed without anyone asking; other attributes get indexed when declared.

nodes.label: BMessages
nodes.rationale: Drag a colour onto the desktop and it changes colour; drag the same colour into a text editor and it inserts the hex value. Neither app was programmed to talk to the colour picker. In Kosmos these are Lua tables with a type field, and they are the same thing that travels between servers.

nodes.label: Direct Graphics Access / BDirectWindow
nodes.rationale: The direct ancestor of Kosmos surfaces. A design detail worth copying: in BeOS it was opt-in and the programmer had to do extra work to use it. Same in Kosmos.

nodes.label: A scripting architecture, not a scripting solution
nodes.rationale: The most valuable idea in the book and the one that was missing. Be provided named hooks rather than a language, so every BeOS app had basic scripting without being written for it. In Kosmos an app exposes its hooks as nodes in its own namespace - fs.write("/app/paint/color", 0xff0000) - so there is no scripting API, no hooks as a separate concept and no new language.

nodes.label: Entity files (BeOS People files)
nodes.rationale: Files with no content - just a name and attributes. Drag one into a mail client and it knows you want to send mail; into a fax program and it goes out over the fax number. It fits Kosmos because a namespace node already returns a table.

nodes.label: BeOS was POSIX-compatible; Kosmos is not
nodes.rationale: BeOS could afford POSIX because its resource model was the same old global tree; Kosmos has per-process namespaces and capabilities, and a POSIX personality would destroy both. The cost is real - BeOS had an ecosystem of ported software and Kosmos will have none - and is accepted in exchange for the result of the experiment.

nodes.label: BeOS was monolithic
nodes.rationale: Drivers, BFS and eventually networking lived inside the kernel, and none of the userland servers could be restarted: killing the app_server took the desktop with it. Kosmos is a real microkernel and supervised restart is a property BeOS did not have.

nodes.label: Threads with shared memory, and the locking API it cost
nodes.rationale: BeOS pushed threads and shared memory into userland and paid with Lock() and Unlock() on every window and an entire class of bugs. Kosmos uses coroutines and share-nothing, and that class of bug does not exist.

nodes.label: The system is usable from the REPL before the app server exists
nodes.rationale: BeOS could not boot into console mode without a GUI and several preferences were only configurable graphically. In Kosmos anything configurable through a graphical interface can be done from the shell, because both speak the same protocol.

nodes.label: The Translation Kit - not copied
nodes.rationale: A central library of translators where a new one extended many apps at once. Good idea, out of scope.

nodes.label: The MediaOS focus - not copied
nodes.rationale: BeOS's whole design was oriented toward real-time video and audio. Kosmos does not have that goal, and the decisions BeOS made for it enter only where they earn their place for another reason.
